intro: Basketball began in a Springfield gym in December 1891. Naismith used peach baskets and a soccer ball and posted thirteen rules. In 1892 the game was played in public and Senda Berenson adapted it at Smith College. The Hall of Fame later stood in Springfield.
The IHSA crowned boys basketball champions beginning in 1908 and girls champions beginning in 1977. Title IX dates to 1972. Gyms are civic rooms. This unit does not teach a dribble.

story.title: Two Baskets on a Balcony
story.kicker: Peach baskets hang at each end of a gym while a class waits underneath.
paragraphs: December 1891. The class cannot go outside. James Naismith needs a game that works under a roof and does not wreck the gym. The reading keeps the name, the place, and the date together.
He asks the building superintendent for boxes. The man brings two peach baskets. They are nailed to the balcony rail. The reading keeps the name, the place, and the date together.
The ball is a soccer ball. The goals are above the players' heads. The game is not soccer and not baseball. It is a new indoor room. The reading keeps the name, the place, and the date together.
Thirteen typed rules go on the bulletin board. Later writers printed those rules. The gym game had paper from the first week. The reading keeps the name, the place, and the date together.

lessons.title: Naismith's Problem
lessons.mainIdea: James Naismith invented basketball in December 1891 because winter closed the fields.
reading: James Naismith taught at the International YMCA Training School in Springfield, Massachusetts. In December 1891 his class needed an indoor game.
Outdoor football was too rough for the small gym. He wanted a game that used skill more than a pile of bodies.
He later wrote that story in Basketball: Its Origin and Development, published in 1941.

lessons.title: Peach Baskets and a Soccer Ball
lessons.mainIdea: The first goals were peach baskets. The first ball was a soccer ball.
reading: Naismith asked for boxes to use as goals. Many tellings say the superintendent brought two peach baskets instead.
The baskets were closed at the bottom. After each goal someone had to get the ball out.
Players threw a soccer ball. A special basketball came later. The first gym game borrowed the ball it already had.

lessons.title: Thirteen Rules
lessons.mainIdea: Naismith typed thirteen rules and posted them for the class.
reading: Naismith wrote thirteen rules. They said the ball could be thrown or batted, but not carried. They said there was no shouldering or tackling.
The rules also said a foul could send a player out until the next goal. The list was short enough to hang on a wall.
Those thirteen rules are not today's full high school book. They are the first paper of the gym game.

lessons.title: A Public Game in 1892
lessons.mainIdea: A public basketball game was played in Springfield in 1892.
reading: The new game did not stay inside one class. In 1892 Springfield saw public basketball games.
YMCA students who finished training took the rules to other gyms. That is how the game left Massachusetts so fast.
The Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame later rose in Springfield to mark that origin on purpose.

lessons.title: Closed Basket to Open Hoop
lessons.mainIdea: Later goals opened at the bottom so the ball could fall through.
reading: Closed peach baskets were slow. People cut the bottoms and then used open hoops with nets.
The change is a design story. It is not a playbook. A hole in the goal changed the rhythm of the game.
A modern hoop is still a high target at each end of a court. That idea is older than the metal rim.

lessons.title: The First Intercollegiate Game
lessons.mainIdea: Minnesota State School of Agriculture beat Hamline 9-3 on 9 February 1895 in an early college game.
reading: On 9 February 1895, the Minnesota State School of Agriculture beat Hamline 9-3. Many histories call this the first intercollegiate basketball game.
The score was small. The game was only a few years old. Colleges were already copying the gym rules.
Springfield 1891 is the invention. 1895 is a college-to-college date.

lessons.mainIdea: The first basketball constitution was thirteen sentences on a wall.
reading: Unlike soccer's later thick Laws, Naismith's first list was brief. A class could see all of it at once.
Short paper travels. Students leaving Springfield could recopy thirteen rules more easily than a long book.
Later handbooks grew. The first paper stayed famous because it was the start.

lessons.title: Backboards Appear
lessons.mainIdea: Clubs added wooden backboards so balcony fans could not interfere with the shot.
reading: Early gyms had balconies. Spectators could reach in and bat the ball. Clubs put wooden boards behind the baskets.
The backboard began as a shield, not as a tool for banking shots. The board then became part of the goal.
A modern rectangle behind the hoop still marks that change.

story.title: A Second Handbook
story.kicker: A Smith College teacher writes a different set of rules for her students.
paragraphs: The Springfield game was not the only paper for long. In 1892 Senda Berenson adapted basketball at Smith College. The reading keeps the name, the place, and the date together.
Her rules divided the court into zones. The women's game had its own handbook, not only a copy of Naismith's list. The reading keeps the name, the place, and the date together.
Illinois schools later built gyms and joined IHSA series. Boys basketball crowned a first state champion in 1908. Girls basketball crowned a first champion in 1977.
The Y sent the seed. School boards heated the rooms. Two dates, 1908 and 1977, mark Illinois paper, not the invention itself. The reading keeps the name, the place, and the date together.
story.think: Why might one invention need more than one rule book?

lessons.title: Senda Berenson at Smith College
lessons.mainIdea: In 1892 Senda Berenson adapted basketball for women at Smith College.
reading: Senda Berenson taught physical education at Smith College in Northampton, Massachusetts. In 1892 she adapted Naismith's game for her students.
Her rules divided the court into zones so players stayed in sections. The women's game had its own paper.
Berenson's work matters because the gym game split early. One invention became more than one handbook.

lessons.title: Who Heats the Gym
lessons.mainIdea: Basketball needed a heated indoor room a town or school would pay for.
reading: Without a gym, Naismith's game has no winter home. Parks close at dusk and freeze.
School boards later built gyms for class and for night games. Those rooms made Friday basketball possible in Illinois towns.
The civic fact is the same as the lighted football field: people paid together for a shared floor.
